# Matakabhattajātaka (Ja 18)

**ID:** Ja 18
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Matakabhattajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Feasts for the Dead
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja18

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Matakabhattajātaka* (Ja 18) is a story in the Pali Jātaka collection (Ekanipāta) [Appleton 2010; SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the frame story concerns the contemporary practice of slaughtering goats, sheep, and other animals to provide a ritual feast for deceased ancestors (*matakabhatta*) [SuttaCentral]. When the monks question the Buddha about the spiritual efficacy of such sacrifices, the Master delivers the story of the past to demonstrate the severe kammic fruition of harming living beings [SuttaCentral; IBC 2011].

In the story of the past, a Brahmin prepares a sacrificial goat, which unexpectedly laughs and then weeps [Yu 2004; Appleton 2010]. Upon being questioned, the animal reveals that five hundred births ago it was a Brahmin who sacrificed goats; having finally reached the end of five hundred successive rebirths of being beheaded as karmic retribution, it laughs with relief [Yu 2004; Appleton 2010]. However, it weeps out of compassion for the Brahmin, who faces the exact same retributive suffering if he proceeds with the slaughter [Yu 2004; Appleton 2010]. Though the Brahmin relents and attempts to safeguard the animal, karmic consequence cannot be averted [Appleton 2010]. The Bodhisatta appears in the narrative as a wise commentator or teacher who articulates the moral lesson [Appleton 2010].

The narrative is frequently cited in Buddhist ethical discourse to illustrate non-violence, the prohibition of animal sacrifice, the severity of *pāṇātipāta* (taking life), and rebirth across realms [Yu 2004; IBC 2011; Fielding 2008]. Modern discussions note that the Dhammapada commentary contains a closely related story (Dhp-a v. 1c, the story of the woman and the ewe) incorporating the common motif of the laugh and cry [Burlingame 1921]. Neither curated parallels nor automated matches (score ≥ 10) are listed for Ja 18 in DharmaNexus or SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].

- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus parallel matching data — Confirmed lack of automated Pali-internal and cross-language text reuse matches.

- [Yu 2004] Yu Xue, Buddhism, War and Nationalism: Chinese Monks in the Struggle Against Japan 1931–1945 (2004) — Discussed the story's use as a standard illustration of non-violence, cause and effect, and animal retribution.
- [Burlingame 1921] Eugene Watson Burlingame, Buddhist Legends: Translated from the Original Pali Text of the Dhammapada Commentary (1921) — Identified the parallel motif (woman and ewe, Dhp-a v. 1c) and the 'Laugh and Cry' motif matching Ja 18 (i. 166–168).
